newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia's King Sihanouk casts doubt on abdication.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's King Sihanouk casts doubt on abdication.

text.p: Cambodia's King Norodom Sihanouk has attempted to defuse controversy over his future role, saying he is not considering abdicating, a statement released by the royal palace said on Tuesday.
But he said the fragile coalition government between the royalist FUNCINPEC party and the formerly communist Cambodian People's Party (CPP) was effectively dead and would disintegrate.

"I am no longer talking of abdicating, because some important compatriots maintain I do not have the right to abdicate and others fear my abdication. I do not want to displease these important compatriots," he said in a statement dated Monday but released by the palace on Tuesday.

Sihanouk, who is in Beijing for medical treatment, whipped up a political storm in February after he said he was no longer happy on the throne and was considering abdicating because of mounting attacks on the monarchy.
The possibility of Sihanouk stepping down added to tension between co-Premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen. The two are to face each other in national polls to be held by 1998.

Hun Sen's CPP party feared the immensely popular Sihanouk would enter politics and bolster the electoral prospects of FUNCINPEC and Ranariddh. Hun Sen threatened to postpone the polls and said he wanted all royal family banned from politics.

Ranariddh, the king's son, angrily defended royalist politics and said he would support Sihanouk if he decided to enter the arena. Sihanouk, meanwhile, said he had no plans to enter politics if he abdicated.

Tuesday's announcement attempted to put that debate to rest. The king stressed his decision to remain on the throne, saying in the statement: "On my death, as King of Cambodia, the Throne Council will alone be responsible for electing a new king."

The council groups the country's two premiers, the parliament chief and his two deputies and the chief monks of the two major Buddhist sects. It must choose a successor to the king within four days of his death or abdication.
The co-Premiers formed an uneasy coalition after U.N.-run elections in 1993, but relations between the two leaders have lurched from crisis to crisis over the past few months.

Hun Sen's open support for royal dissidents challenging Ranariddh's leadership earlier this month sparked rumours of an imminent coup, but tensions eased after the leaders and their military and police chiefs last week agreed to avoid violence.
But Sihanouk, in released annotations to news stories written at the height of the latest crisis, wrote that the royal coalition government (RGC) was all but dead and FUNCINPEC was doomed.
"The RCG is already practically dead," he wrote. "The RCG is inevitably going to disintegrate," the king said about news stories published on April 17 and 18.
